lesson.title: Wrong Kind of Thing: Understanding TypeError
lesson.summary: TypeError means an operation was asked to work with a combination of types it simply is not defined for, regardless of what specific value those types happen to hold.
lesson.body:
Every value in Python has a type: an int, a float, a str, a list, and so on, and many operations are only defined for certain combinations of types. TypeError is Python's way of reporting exactly that situation: the operation you asked for makes no sense given the types involved, no matter what specific values those types happen to contain. It is entirely about type, the kind of thing a value is, not about whatever particular value is inside it.

Here is a classic example. Suppose age was read in from somewhere as text, so it holds the string "16" rather than the int 16, and the code tries to add 1 to it directly.

```python
age = "16"
print(age + 1)
```

Running this prints a traceback whose final line is:

```
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

The + operator does have a meaning for two strings (it joins them together) and a separate meaning for two numbers (it adds them), but Python defines no meaning at all for a str combined with an int, so this fails immediately every single time, no matter what the string actually says. Even age = "abc" would raise the exact same TypeError for the exact same reason, because the problem is entirely about the types str and int being combined with +, not about whether "16" happens to look like a number. The fix is to convert age to the matching type first, using int(), the same conversion tool you already know from working with type conversion.

```python
age = "16"
print(int(age) + 1)
```

This prints:

```
17
```

Once age is converted to the int 16, adding 1 is perfectly well defined, and the code works. Other everyday examples of TypeError include calling len() on an int, which has no length, or trying to index into an int with square brackets, which is not a sequence at all.

Keep this distinction close at hand as you move to the next chapter: TypeError shows up when the kind of thing you have is simply wrong for what you are trying to do with it, and no particular value of that wrong type would have worked either. That is different from a case where the type is exactly right for the operation, but the specific value inside it is not usable, which is precisely what the next chapter, ValueError, is about.
